planting.note: Transplant nursery-propagated stock in spring into dry, deep, sandy, acidic, well-drained soil in full sun; scarify seed before starting indoors, as germination is otherwise slow and erratic.

directions: Scareweed is a rare wild indigo endemic to deep, dry, fire-maintained sandhills and scrub of the Florida Panhandle, distinguished from most of its Baptisia relatives by simple, undivided leaves rather than the typical three-parted leaflets. It forms a low, sprawling mound topped with pale yellow pea flowers in spring, followed by inflated seed pods, and depends on excessively drained, nutrient-poor sand that would rot most other perennials. Source only nursery-propagated plants from native plant specialists, since wild populations are limited and seed-grown plants can take two to three years to reach blooming size. Once established its deep taproot makes it extremely drought tolerant and essentially maintenance-free in the right sandy site.

planting.note: Direct sow fresh seed in fall into dry, deep, sandy, acidic, well-drained soil in full sun; the corm forms slowly and prefers the same fire-maintained sandhill and flatwoods conditions where it occurs naturally.

directions: Fewflower Blazingstar is a diminutive native of pine flatwoods and sandhills across the Southeastern Coastal Plain from Florida to South Carolina, named for its sparse arrangement of flower heads compared to the densely packed spikes of Liatris spicata. Rosy-purple flower heads open along a short, wiry stem in fall, drawing in native bees and late-season butterflies at a time when many other wildflowers have finished blooming. Its small stature and preference for lean, excessively drained sand make it a good fit for rock gardens or dry meadow plantings rather than typical border soil. Established plants are extremely drought tolerant and rarely need supplemental water once their corm is settled in.

planting.note: Direct sow fresh seed in fall onto thin, rocky, alkaline soil in full sun; this Edwards Plateau endemic expects shallow limestone-derived soils and sharp drainage rather than rich garden loam.

directions: Earle's Blazingstar is a Texas Hill Country endemic restricted to thin, rocky, alkaline soils over limestone on the Edwards Plateau, where it produces compact spikes of rose-purple flower heads in fall. It is rarely offered commercially and best suited to native plant enthusiasts building xeric limestone gardens or rock gardens that mimic its natural glade and outcrop habitat. Like other blazingstars it grows from an underground corm and is extremely drought tolerant once established, but it resents heavy or poorly drained soils that hold winter moisture. Its fall nectar is valuable to native bees and migrating butterflies moving through central Texas.

planting.note: Direct sow fresh seed in fall into rocky, well-drained, alkaline soil in full sun; this central Texas limestone-prairie native does poorly in heavy clay or soil that stays wet.

directions: Cluster Blazingstar takes its name from the swollen, turgid involucral bracts that cup each tightly clustered flower head along its upright spike, a distinguishing feature for this limestone-prairie native of central Texas. Rose-purple blooms open in fall above narrow, grass-like foliage, providing a late nectar source for bees and butterflies on the Blackland and Edwards Plateau prairies where it grows. It thrives on thin, rocky, calcareous soils and full sun, and like its relatives it forms an underground corm that stores energy through summer drought. It is uncommon in cultivation but well suited to xeric native plantings that replicate its limestone-glade habitat.

planting.note: Direct sow seed on bare soil in fall so winter cold naturally stratifies it; unlike moisture-loving eastern ironweeds this Great Plains species needs well-drained upland soil and should not be kept consistently wet.

directions: Plains Ironweed is the most drought-tolerant of the ironweeds, native to dry upland prairies and roadsides across the central Great Plains from Nebraska and Kansas south into Oklahoma and Texas. Its foliage carries a whitish, cottony margin and undersurface that sets it apart at a glance from the darker, moisture-loving ironweeds of the eastern prairies, and a deep taproot lets it shrug off the heat and drought typical of shortgrass and mixed-grass prairie summers. Rounded clusters of magenta-purple flowers open in late summer atop shorter, sturdier stems than tall ironweed, making it less prone to flopping in a dry border. It pairs well with other shortgrass prairie natives like blue grama and prairie coneflower and draws bees and butterflies during the late-season nectar dearth.
